title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models
authors: Ivan Moloshnikov, Dmitry Kunitsyn, Alexander Sboev, Maksim Skorokhodov, Roman Rybka, Yuanchao Liu
abstract: Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles---analyst, coder, and recorder~---with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged. The approach is validated in two directions: tuning a classification spiking neural network with correlation learning, and solving high-order differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). Across five tasks---spiking classification on MNIST and Digits, and boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky (KS) equations---the agent outperforms the baselines: classification accuracy is 13 percentage points (MNIST) and 6 percentage points (Digits) higher; the error against the analytical single-soliton solution is reduced approximately 2491-fold; the invariant-preservation error drops approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE run with a Gaussian perturbation and by more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations; and the mass drift drops 14-fold for the KS problem with a Gaussian perturbation. The framework thus tunes key components on tasks of different nature without changing its internal structure.

infographic.key_insight: A three-agent LLM loop can automatically tune only the critical components of specialized neural models while keeping the overall architecture fixed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a transferable workflow for improving domain-specific ML systems without full architecture search or manual hyperparameter tuning.
method: Analyst identifies the component to optimize and defines the tuning target.
Coder generates code only for the allowed model component inside a sandbox.
Recorder logs each trial, result, and decision to guide iterative refinement.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five tasks, the system improved spiking classification on MNIST and Digits and reduced errors/drift dramatically on GNLSE and KS PDE benchmarks, including a ~2491-fold error reduction in one GNLSE run.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on sandboxed code generation and a carefully constrained search space, so robustness may vary when components or task specifications are less clearly defined.
infographic.paper_title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models

title: Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training
authors: Chenxu Zhang, Yaorui Shi, Wenlong Zhang, Jianchao Tan, Zihan Wang, Yiming Cheng
abstract: Training long-horizon language model agents requires assigning credit to intermediate decisions from sparse terminal feedback. Within a finite group of sibling rollouts, useful action comparisons depend on their context, evidence for both alternatives, and how that evidence enters learning. We propose Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization (MCGPO), a procedure for constructing weighted action preferences from already collected trajectories. MCGPO defines comparison contexts with pre-action state summaries and observed rubric progress, annotated by task rules. Two-action support selects among ordered exact and coarse matching rules. Fixed folds separate candidate decisions from the terminal outcomes used to orient their preferences, and support-dependent evidence weights scale an auxiliary pairwise objective alongside shared GraphGPO task learning. MCGPO reuses rollout data and each response's original history, preserving critic-free training. Across six environment-backbone settings with three training seeds each, MCGPO improves mean success over matched GraphGPO: by 0.47-1.46 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B, and by 3.96 and 5.16 points on WebShop with Qwen3-4B and 8B. The ALFWorld gains build on baseline success above 92%, where remaining headroom is limited. Integrated success improves in three of four Qwen2.5 settings. Three-seed factorial controls support opposite-fold evidence and evidence weighting; joint state-rubric matching achieves the highest mean in all four representation-control settings.

infographic.key_insight: MCGPO improves LLM agent training by turning already-collected sibling rollouts into context-matched action preferences with rubric-aware evidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a critic-free, data-efficient way to assign intermediate credit in long-horizon agents while reusing rollout history and terminal feedback.
method: Build comparison contexts from pre-action state summaries plus observed rubric progress.
Use two-action support with ordered exact/coarse matching to select valid action pairs.
Apply fixed folds and support-dependent weights to orient preferences and train alongside GraphGPO.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six environment-backbone settings and three seeds each, MCGPO improves mean success over matched GraphGPO on ALFWorld and WebShop, with the largest gains on WebShop using Qwen3-4B and 8B.
infographic.watch_item: The gains on ALFWorld are modest because baseline success is already above 92%, so remaining improvement headroom is limited.
infographic.paper_title: Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training

title: Goal-Oriented Bundle Management and Flow Control for Deep-Space Communications via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Sajjad Baghaeea, Aimin Lib, Shanmugarajan Balasubramanian, Elif Uysal
abstract: Deep-space communications operate under intermittent connectivity, long propagation delays, and relay storage constraints. In such networks, the Bundle Protocol enables store-carry-forward communication, requiring relay nodes to manage limited storage and scarce contact opportunities. Relay-side scheduling and dropping decisions are inherently goal-oriented: transmission resources should be allocated to bundles most valuable to downstream mission objectives. Conventional schedulers, such as FIFO, do not explicitly optimize task utility and may provide unfair service across heterogeneous planetary sources. This paper presents a closed-loop modeling and learning framework for relay-side bundle and flow management in a contact-driven deep-space network, where lunar and Martian updates are forwarded through a shared-buffer relay to Earth. We quantify destination-side information freshness using excess age $Δ_i^e(t)=[Δ_i(t)-d_i(t)]^+$, where $Δ_i(t)$ denotes the Age of Information of source $i$ and $d_i(t)$ is a source-dependent delay baseline. Based on this metric, we define a goal-oriented loss that supports source-dependent nonlinear penalties, allowing prioritization according to mission relevance. We formulate relay control as a constrained semi-Markov decision process (CSMDP) and solve it using masked Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Feasibility-aware action masking restricts transmissions to bundles that can complete within the remaining contact window. DTNSim simulations indicate improved age-based utility and inter-flow fairness compared with baseline schedulers. The proposed framework jointly optimizes relay-side bundle scheduling, dropping, and flow control under contact-driven dynamics with explicit fairness considerations across heterogeneous sources.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns deep-space relay scheduling into a goal-oriented reinforcement learning problem that prioritizes bundles by mission value, freshness, and fairness rather than simple FIFO order.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is directly useful for deep-space network relays because it provides a control strategy for scarce storage and intermittent contacts while improving delivery utility across heterogeneous planetary sources.
method: Model relay control as a constrained semi-Markov decision process (CSMDP).
Use masked Lagrangian PPO to learn scheduling, dropping, and flow-control policies.
Apply feasibility-aware action masking so only bundles that can finish within the remaining contact window are transmitted.
infographic.evidence_signal: DTNSim simulations reported better age-based utility and inter-flow fairness than baseline schedulers such as FIFO.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on accurate contact-window prediction and the ability of the learned policy to generalize across different deep-space traffic patterns and mission priority settings.
infographic.paper_title: Goal-Oriented Bundle Management and Flow Control for Deep-Space Communications via Reinforcement Learning

title: PhySeqNet: physics-informed fluorescent foci detection for BARseq spatial transcriptomics
authors: Neha Goswami, John Hover, Renae Galluccio, Yichen Wu, Huiqing Zhan, Xiaoyin Chen
abstract: BARseq enables spatially resolved gene-expression profiling across intact tissue, but its sensitivity depends on accurate detection and decoding of dense fluorescent rolonies. Existing spot-calling approaches can be conservative where signals overlap, while supervised deep learning is limited by the lack of reliable manual ground truth in real tissue images. Here we present PhySeqNet, a physics-informed deep learning framework for annotation-free fluorescent foci detection in BARseq. PhySeqNet trains U-Net detectors entirely on semi-synthetic images generated from an instrument-matched optical model combined with real sample-free experimental noise, and is integrated into pyBARseq, a modular Python pipeline for BARseq analysis. PhySeqNet achieved high detection performance on held-out simulated data across wavelength bands. On real tissue images, where ground truth is unavailable, we evaluated detections by forward-model reconstruction: PhySeqNet with conservative barcode-aware non-maxima suppression (NMSB) achieved higher reconstruction fidelity (NCC and MS-SSIM) than the BarDensr single-shot estimator, tuned classical spot detectors, and a pretrained deep-learning detector. In the analyzed brain section, PhySeqNet with NMSB yielded a median of 51 counts per cell versus 47 for BarDensr, with a similar number of genes detected per cell. The recovered transcripts produced spatial expression patterns qualitatively consistent with Allen MERFISH reference data and preserved cell-type composition after scANVI label transfer. These results show that physics-informed simulation can train practical, annotation-free detectors that improve BARseq sensitivity without disrupting downstream biological interpretation.

infographic.key_insight: PhySeqNet uses physics-informed synthetic training to detect fluorescent BARseq foci without manual annotation, improving sensitivity in dense tissue images.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a practical, modular detector for spatial transcriptomics pipelines that can be deployed where real ground truth is unavailable.
method: Trains a U-Net on semi-synthetic images generated from an instrument-matched optical model plus real experimental noise.
Integrates barcode-aware non-maxima suppression (NMSB) to reduce duplicate detections in crowded regions.
Built as part of pyBARseq for end-to-end BARseq analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: On real tissue, reconstruction-based evaluation showed higher fidelity than BarDensr, tuned classical spot detectors, and a pretrained deep-learning detector, with a median 51 counts per cell versus 47 for BarDensr.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on real tissue is inferred indirectly through forward-model reconstruction because reliable manual ground truth is unavailable.
infographic.paper_title: PhySeqNet: physics-informed fluorescent foci detection for BARseq spatial transcriptomics

title: Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization via Zeroth-Order Residual Tracking
authors: El Mahdi Chayti, Alireza Mirrokni, Martin Jaggi
abstract: Many optimization problems provide direct access to only part of the gradient, while the remaining component must be inferred from function evaluations. This structure arises in performative prediction, performative reinforcement learning, and bilevel optimization with a black-box lower level. We introduce Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization (PISO), which combines the available gradient component with a running estimate of the residual. By centring each zeroth-order observation on this estimate, PISO makes the variance due to random probing depend on the tracking error rather than the residual's magnitude. This yields a randomized sketch iteration with an explicit contraction mechanism and a principled interpretation of momentum. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish convergence guarantees that depend on the residual's variation and initial magnitude, without requiring a uniform bound on the unavailable gradient component. With independently sampled function evaluations and Gaussian or spherical probes, PISO attains leading function-evaluation complexities of \(O(d^{2}\varepsilon^{-6})\) under Lipschitz gradients and \(O(d^{2}\varepsilon^{-5})\) under an additional Lipschitz-Hessian assumption. These rates require only one probe direction, two function samples, and one known-component sample per update. The analysis also quantifies how batching trades observations for fewer deployments. Across five settings, PISO variants improve on the tested baselines with comparable oracle access in three, reach a comparable solution faster in bilevel routing, and perform best among methods without response-model derivatives in performative reinforcement learning.

infographic.key_insight: PISO combines the known gradient part with a tracked estimate of the unknown residual, so zeroth-order noise is controlled by tracking error rather than by the full missing gradient magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes partially observed optimization practical for systems like performative learning, RL, and bilevel problems where only some derivatives are available and function evaluations are expensive.
method: Uses the available gradient component directly and updates a running estimate of the residual.
Centers each zeroth-order probe on the residual estimate to reduce variance and create a contraction step.
Supports Gaussian or spherical probes with just one probe direction, two function samples, and one known-gradient sample per iteration.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence rates of O(d^2ε^-6) with Lipschitz gradients and O(d^2ε^-5) with an additional Lipschitz-Hessian assumption, plus empirical gains across five benchmark settings.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the residual-tracking quality and on independently sampled function evaluations, so noisy or correlated oracle calls may weaken the method's advantages.
infographic.paper_title: Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization via Zeroth-Order Residual Tracking

title: Dream to Remember: Continual Steering of Generalist Robot Policies with World Models
authors: Bahey Tharwat, Iman Nematollahi, Marvin Alles, Xingyuan Zhang, Akshay L Chandra, Abhinav Valada
abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained with imitation learning and are bounded by the quality and coverage of their demonstrations. Reinforcement learning can improve and extend them, either by fine-tuning the policy weights or by training a small module to steer the input noise of a frozen generative policy. When tasks arrive sequentially, both approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning on a task degrades prior tasks, and steering only shifts forgetting to the shared steering module. We propose Dream to Remember (D2R), which continually steers a frozen generalist policy toward new tasks, while retaining its earlier skills. As the steering module learns a new task, a frozen pretrained world model rehearses prior tasks through imagined rollouts, anchoring the module to its earlier behavior without a replay buffer or new data. When the world model is faithful enough, D2R learns the new task entirely in imagination. Otherwise, it learns the task in the environment while using the world model only to rehearse prior tasks. On CALVIN, D2R improves eight tasks in sequence entirely in imagination, raising average success from 63.7% to 74.8%, while LoRA fine-tuning on the same sequence drops it to 11.7%. With a frozen off-the-shelf generalist policy and world model, $π_0$ and A2World, D2R learns unseen LIBERO-90 tasks in the environment while keeping $π_0$'s performance on the LIBERO suites it was fine-tuned on, even though the world model is not accurate enough for policy optimization. Finally, on a real Franka robot, D2R improves three tasks in sequence entirely in imagination while retaining the earlier improvements.

infographic.key_insight: Dream to Remember (D2R) continually adapts a frozen generalist robot policy to new tasks while preventing catastrophic forgetting by rehearsing prior behaviors through a frozen world model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical continual-learning recipe for robotics that improves task adaptation without replay buffers, while preserving prior robot skills across sequential updates.
method: Freeze the base generalist policy and learn only a lightweight steering module.
Use a pretrained world model to generate imagined rollouts that rehearse earlier tasks.
Train new tasks in imagination when the world model is accurate enough; otherwise, train in the environment while the world model anchors past behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across CALVIN, D2R raised average success from 63.7% to 74.8% over eight sequential tasks in imagination, while LoRA fine-tuning fell to 11.7%; it also retained prior performance on LIBERO and improved three real-robot Franka tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the fidelity of the frozen world model, so weak model predictions may limit optimization quality and shift training back to real-environment learning.
infographic.paper_title: Dream to Remember: Continual Steering of Generalist Robot Policies with World Models

title: Studying Comics at Scale with Artificial Intelligence: The PAGE Framework and Three Studies of American Comics and Japanese Manga
authors: Emilio Ferrara
abstract: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.

infographic.key_insight: The PAGE framework uses AI to parse, annotate, and explain comics at archive scale, enabling new quantitative studies of visual storytelling across American comics and Japanese manga.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This paper shows how multimodal document AI can transform large, scanned cultural archives into searchable, analyzable datasets while preserving links to human-coded validation.
method: Parse every page into panels, text, and bibliographic metadata
Use a vision-language model guided by a written codebook for page annotations
Ground model outputs with human annotation and estimate change while controlling for publisher and genre
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework is demonstrated on 3,929 American comic books (1938–1956) and 87 Japanese manga volumes across three studies, with results checked against human annotation.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality of scans and codebook consistency, and archive-level comparisons must account for publisher and genre confounding.
infographic.paper_title: Studying Comics at Scale with Artificial Intelligence: The PAGE Framework and Three Studies of American Comics and Japanese Manga

title: Pretraining and Test-Time Training Budgets Matter for ARC: A Controlled Study of VARC and TRM
authors: Adrien Deliege, Marc Van Droogenbroeck
abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is increasingly used to evaluate whether neural networks can infer task-specific transformations from few demonstrations. Recent ARC models differ in architecture, but also in broader training and evaluation protocols, including pretraining data, data augmentation, test-time setup, and optimization budgets, making conclusions about architecture benefits debatable. In this work, we study how the performance of the vision-inspired VARC and recursion-based TRM models is affected by pretraining and test-time training (TTT) budgets under a common inductive protocol on ARC-AGI-1. We cross five pretraining budgets with four TTT budgets for each test task. Each budget specifies a task-variant count and total sample presentations, defining the controlled training budgets. We observe that increasing TTT sample presentations improves the standard ARC pass@2 metric in all settings for both models. Increasing the TTT task-variant count consistently helps only TRM, whereas VARC often performs better with fewer variants. VARC also remains competitive without pretraining, while TRM benefits much more from it. These results show that pretraining and TTT budgets affect ARC evaluation and motivate reporting at comparable budgets.

infographic.key_insight: On ARC-AGI-1, both pretraining and test-time training budgets materially change model performance, so architecture comparisons between VARC and TRM must be interpreted through the lens of matched training budgets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For engineering teams building few-shot reasoning systems, the study shows that optimizing pretraining and test-time adaptation budgets can matter as much as model design when chasing ARC gains.
method: Crossed 5 pretraining budgets with 4 test-time training (TTT) budgets per test task.
Evaluated VARC and TRM under the same inductive protocol on ARC-AGI-1.
Tracked task-variant count and total sample presentations as controlled budget variables.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that increasing TTT sample presentations improves pass@2 for both models, while more task variants consistently help TRM but often hurt or fail to help VARC.
infographic.watch_item: Results are tied to a specific ARC-AGI-1 setup and controlled budget grid, so gains may not transfer directly to other datasets or unconstrained evaluation protocols.
infographic.paper_title: Pretraining and Test-Time Training Budgets Matter for ARC: A Controlled Study of VARC and TRM

title: Calibration in One Go: Jointly Learning Accurate and Calibrated Neural Networks
authors: Nektarios Kalampalikis, Pablo M. Olmos, Isabel Valera
abstract: Neural networks (NNs), while highly flexible and versatile, are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration methods adjust the outputs of an already trained model using a separate calibration dataset and additional calibration parameters. This process adds overhead that requires separate optimization of the calibrator and subsequent model selection. In this paper, we show that standard (post-hoc) calibrators can be trained end-to-end with the backbone via a bilevel Stackelberg formulation. This formulation eliminates the need for a separate calibration set or a dedicated calibration loss by jointly optimizing accuracy and calibration using cross-entropy, introducing only one additional hyperparameter: the calibrator learning rate. Although our framework supports calibrators ranging from temperature and matrix scaling to NN layers, our results show that using the final classification layer itself as the calibrator yields accurate, well-calibrated models with no additional parameters. Our approach outperforms SOTA calibrators with minimal added complexity, while also avoiding the multiplicative overhead of separate calibration components in settings such as multi-task learning.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that neural network accuracy and calibration can be learned jointly in one training loop, removing the need for separate post-hoc calibration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This simplifies deployment by eliminating a dedicated calibration set and extra calibrator optimization, while improving reliability of model probabilities.
method: Formulate calibration as a bilevel Stackelberg optimization problem trained end-to-end with the backbone.
Use standard calibrators such as temperature scaling, matrix scaling, or neural layers within the joint objective.
Find that the final classification layer can act as the calibrator with no extra parameters.
evidence_signal
infographic.paper_title: Calibration in One Go: Jointly Learning Accurate and Calibrated Neural Networks

title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
authors: Taoyong Cui, Pinxian Zeng, Wanghan Xu, Hao Xiao, Shuhan Xue, Qiang Gao
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI-Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.

infographic.key_insight: RSI-Anything turns interaction data into persistent gains by using predictive world models to select actions and update policies only when improvements remain compatible and reliable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical, domain-general recipe for continuous improvement in systems like code repair, GUI agents, and lab planning without depending solely on expensive external feedback.
method: Use a JEPA-based world model to predict outcomes of candidate actions.
Select learning data and actions based on predicted utility, then adapt the world model conditionally.
Retain updated policy-model pairs only after component and compatibility checks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple benchmarks, the method improved outcomes such as code repair success (26.3% to 31.2%), GUI efficiency (39.4% fewer actions), lab-planning scores (21.80% to 46.01%), and reaction optimization yield (96.15% vs. 82.16%).
infographic.watch_item: Because the approach depends on predictive world models, performance may degrade if model drift or environment changes make predictions unreliable.
infographic.paper_title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models

title: Constrained Probabilistic Numerics: Gaussian Process Solvers for Linear PDEs under Linear Inequality Constraints
authors: Boyuan Deng, Kshitiz Upadhyay, Michael Shields
abstract: Gaussian process solvers for linear partial differential equations (PDEs) return posteriors rather than point estimates, but they condition only on equality information: the PDE residual, boundary data, and measurements. Many solutions of interest also obey inequality constraints, including nonnegativity, monotonicity, and absence of arbitrage, which equality conditioning cannot enforce. We prove that conditioning a Gaussian process prior jointly on linear equality observations and a finite-dimensional inequality event is equivalent to conditioning sequentially in terms of Borel measures on the solution space. The physics-informed posterior is therefore a valid prior for the inequality update at virtual points. The combined law is non-Gaussian yet computable through truncated-Gaussian moments, and neither the PDE conditioning nor the inequality update requires modification. We evaluated the construction on a Poisson benchmark, option-price surfaces, and air-quality fields. Under incomplete boundary data, a monotonicity constraint lowered the error of a two-dimensional Poisson reconstruction by $63\%$. On a real S&P 500 option chain thinned to $20$ retained quotes, no-arbitrage constraints reduced held-out extrapolation error by $22\%$ and cut the calendar-arbitrage rate from $10\%$ to $1\%$. On four real air-quality snapshots, nonnegativity reduced a Gaussian moment-based sub-zero-tail proxy by $74\%$ at the sparsest monitor count. Changes in mean accuracy and constraint diagnostics differed across data regimes. The probability of the noisy virtual constraint event under the equality posterior measures agreement with the specified bounds before the update. The construction turns admissibility from a post-processing step into conditioning information for probabilistic PDE solvers.

infographic.key_insight: Inequality constraints can be incorporated directly into Gaussian process PDE solvers as a valid sequential conditioning step, turning admissibility requirements like positivity, monotonicity, and no-arbitrage into part of the probabilistic update.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical way to enforce physically or economically meaningful constraints in scientific computing without changing the underlying PDE solver pipeline.
method: Condition a GP prior on PDE residuals, boundary data, and measurements to form a physics-informed posterior.
Treat finite-dimensional inequality constraints as a second conditioning step via truncated-Gaussian moments.
Use the equality-conditioned posterior as the prior for virtual inequality observations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Poisson reconstruction, option pricing, and air-quality experiments, the constrained approach improved errors and constraint satisfaction, including a 63% error reduction on Poisson, 22% lower extrapolation error on thin S&P 500 option data, and a 74% reduction in sub-zero-tail proxy for air-quality fields.
infographic.watch_item: The inequality update is computationally non-Gaussian and depends on virtual-point choices and truncated-moment calculations, which may affect scalability and numerical stability.
infographic.paper_title: Constrained Probabilistic Numerics: Gaussian Process Solvers for Linear PDEs under Linear Inequality Constraints

title: Amortized Counterfactual Prediction with Graph Neural Networks
authors: Hendrik Stumpf, Francesco Quinzan
abstract: Counterfactual inference asks how an observed outcome might have differed under different circumstances, such as whether a patient would have recovered had they received a different treatment. Such questions arise whenever decisions depend on the outcomes of alternatives that were not observed. Answering counterfactual queries generally requires knowledge of the underlying causal structure, which is often unavailable in practice. A common approach is therefore to first estimate the causal graph from observational data and then perform counterfactual inference. However, errors in the estimated causal graph can propagate to downstream counterfactual predictions. To address this challenge, we introduce the Counterfactual Graph Neural Process (CFGNP), an end-to-end approach that answers counterfactual queries directly from observational data without first estimating a causal graph. CFGNP uses Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to exploit the dual-graph structure by restricting cross-world message passing to corresponding factual--counterfactual variables. Across synthetic and image-based benchmarks, CFGNP achieves stronger predictive performance than existing approaches, including on the German Loan benchmark, where it reduces MSE from $4.51 \times 10^{-2}$ to $0.19 \times 10^{-2}$. Furthermore, on synthetic causal graphs, a model trained only on 10-node graphs maintains strong predictive performance on graphs with up to 30 nodes, without retraining.

infographic.key_insight: CFGNP learns counterfactual predictions directly from observational data by using a graph neural network to pass messages only between corresponding factual and counterfactual variables, avoiding explicit causal graph estimation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more robust counterfactual decision support in settings like healthcare and lending, where causal structure is uncertain and errors in graph estimation can degrade downstream predictions.
method: End-to-end Counterfactual Graph Neural Process for counterfactual inference
Dual-graph GNN with restricted cross-world message passing between matched variables
Trained on observational data without separately learning a causal graph
infographic.evidence_signal: Across synthetic and image-based benchmarks, including German Loan, CFGNP outperformed prior methods and reduced MSE from 4.51×10^-2 to 0.19×10^-2; a model trained on 10-node graphs generalized to graphs with up to 30 nodes without retraining.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality and coverage of observational training data, and generalization to larger or structurally different causal systems may still be limited in real-world deployments.
infographic.paper_title: Amortized Counterfactual Prediction with Graph Neural Networks

title: X-AVDD: Cross-Attentive Audio-Visual Dataset Distillation
authors: Saumyaranjan Mohanty, Aravind Reddy, Konda Reddy Mopuri
abstract: Audio-visual dataset distillation aims to synthesize a small dataset from a large paired audio-visual dataset, while nearly preserving the training utility for neural networks. Existing approaches such as DM and AVDD face two critical limitations: 1) they are memory-intensive, making them difficult to scale to complex architectures and higher samples-per-class (SPC) settings, and 2) they often fail to preserve strong cross-modal semantic correspondence. To tackle these issues, we propose X-AVDD, a cross-attention-based distillation method that explicitly captures inter-modal relationships during synthesis. By decoupling cross-modal alignment from joint optimization, X-AVDD is substantially more memory-efficient, reducing end-to-end synthesis cost by $\sim 8\times$ GPU-hours, while producing highly aligned synthetic data. Empirically, X-AVDD significantly outperforms other audio-visual distillation methods. On VGGSound, an audio-visual dataset of short YouTube clips, X-AVDD improves top-1 test accuracy from $8.2\%\rightarrow24.0\%$ at SPC=$10$ and $9.8\%\rightarrow26.5\%$ at SPC=$20$. Furthermore, X-AVDD improves cross-architecture generalization (e.g., $25.5\%\rightarrow35.3\%$ for a ViT target on AVE dataset at SPC $=50$) and successfully scales to complex architectures such as AudioCLIP, achieving $62.3\%$ accuracy using only $5.65\%$ of the full dataset, against the full dataset accuracy of $72.4\%$ while completing in $9\times$ lower training time compared to the full dataset.

infographic.key_insight: X-AVDD distills paired audio-visual data by using cross-attention to preserve inter-modal semantics, making synthetic datasets more aligned and much more memory-efficient than prior methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables scalable audio-visual dataset distillation for larger models and higher samples-per-class settings, reducing synthesis cost while retaining strong downstream training utility.
method: Use cross-attention to explicitly model audio-visual correspondence during synthesis.
Decouple cross-modal alignment from joint optimization to reduce memory usage.
Generate compact synthetic paired data that preserves cross-modal semantics for training.
infographic.evidence_signal: On VGGSound, X-AVDD raises top-1 accuracy from 8.2% to 24.0% at SPC=10 and from 9.8% to 26.5% at SPC=20, and it also improves cross-architecture transfer and scales to AudioCLIP with much lower training time.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on carefully maintaining cross-modal alignment during synthesis, so mismatched audio-visual pairing or unstable attention learning could reduce distillation quality.
infographic.paper_title: X-AVDD: Cross-Attentive Audio-Visual Dataset Distillation

title: X-AgentRed: Red-Teaming Personal Agents in Evolving Multi-Service Ecosystems
authors: Yeonsung Jung, Zhiyuan Wang, Zifan Wang, Vítor Albiero, Benjamin Newman, Edoardo Debenedetti
abstract: Personal agents increasingly connect to services across the web and applications by using tools. As the effects of their actions accumulate and interact across services, unintended or harmful outcomes can arise when agents fulfill benign user requests. Proactively identifying these compositional failures requires systematically exploring diverse cross-service paths. Existing red-teaming methods often simply prompt LLMs to identify potentially harmful paths from task and environment descriptions or decompose harmful objectives specified by humans or LLMs into seemingly benign action combinations. However, generation is biased toward patterns learned during training, potentially favoring familiar tool combinations and leaving novel cross-service interactions underexplored. To address this, we propose X-AgentRed, a self-evolving red-teaming framework that discovers harmful tool call paths through a graph of tool dependencies and expands and refines them using execution feedback. By analyzing each tool's effects, potential harms, and preconditions for execution, the red-teaming agent constructs a directed graph that captures how one tool's effects can satisfy another's execution preconditions. Recipes sampled from this graph are instantiated as realistic scenarios in which agents can produce harmful outcomes. Execution feedback enables self-improvement by diversifying paths that produce harm through tool substitution and refining preconditions at blocked steps in unsuccessful paths to enable further execution. Across four frontier agentic models, X-AgentRed achieves $1.77\times$ the harmful path rate of STAC and explores a more diverse set of tools, yielding $2.99\times$ the tool coverage on average.

infographic.key_insight: X-AgentRed finds harmful cross-service agent behaviors by building and evolving a tool-dependency graph instead of relying only on prompted attack generation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For personal agents that act across multiple apps and services, this offers a practical way to stress-test tool chains and uncover risky compositional failures before deployment.
method: Analyze each tool’s effects, harms, and execution preconditions.
Build a directed graph where one tool’s effects can satisfy another tool’s requirements.
Sample graph recipes into realistic scenarios, then use execution feedback to diversify tool substitutions and refine blocked preconditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four frontier agentic models, the method reached 1.77× the harmful path rate of STAC and 2.99× average tool coverage.
infographic.watch_item: Because it relies on modeled tool effects and preconditions, performance may depend on how accurately the ecosystem is described and may miss harms outside the constructed graph.
infographic.paper_title: X-AgentRed: Red-Teaming Personal Agents in Evolving Multi-Service Ecosystems

title: Specialists Learn Faster: Knowledge Organization in Pre-training Shapes Knowledge Update Efficiency
authors: Sheng Zhao, Yuhao Zhu
abstract: An ideal (language) model must continually update its knowledge. Existing work largely focuses on making these updates efficient after training. We investigate how the organization of time-varying knowledge during pre-training shapes the efficiency of subsequent updates. Models trained on chronologically ordered knowledge specialize in the most recently encountered knowledge; we call them specialists. In contrast, models trained on the same knowledge in randomly shuffled order perform well across all represented time periods; we call them generalists. Surprisingly, specialists require far fewer update steps than generalists to acquire new knowledge. To explain this advantage, we derive a law from first principles that relates update cost to the model's optimization dynamics and that closely predicts empirical results. Guided by these findings, we design a strategy for organizing pre-training data that preserves stable historical knowledge while enabling efficient updates to current knowledge. We also show that the benefits of temporal knowledge organization extend to real-world pre-trained models and existing knowledge update tools, and generalize to other knowledge orderings. Project page: https://horizon-lab.org/specialist/

infographic.key_insight: How knowledge is ordered during pre-training changes later update efficiency: models trained chronologically become "specialists" that adapt to new knowledge much faster than randomly shuffled "generalists."
infographic.engineering_relevance: For continually updated language models, pre-training data organization can reduce future update cost while helping preserve useful historical knowledge.
method: Compare chronological vs randomly shuffled pre-training knowledge orderings.
Derive a first-principles law linking update cost to optimization dynamics.
Design a data-ordering strategy that improves stability of past knowledge and update efficiency for current knowledge.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports empirical comparisons on pre-trained models and existing knowledge-update tools, with the derived law closely predicting observed update costs across knowledge orderings.
infographic.watch_item: The benefit depends on temporal structure in the training data, so gains may be weaker or require re-tuning when the data does not have a meaningful chronology.
infographic.paper_title: Specialists Learn Faster: Knowledge Organization in Pre-training Shapes Knowledge Update Efficiency

title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code
authors: Meriem Terki, Nouhaila Innan, Minghao Shao, Muhammad Kashif, Alberto Marchisio, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Generated suites almost always execute, but discrimination lags behind: the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval, so executability alone overstates test quality. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. QTestBench offers a reproducible, cross-framework benchmark for the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.

infographic.key_insight: QTestBench shows that LLM-generated quantum tests often run successfully but still fail to reliably distinguish correct code from buggy code.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum software engineering, the framework provides a practical way to assess whether automated tests are trustworthy before using them in validation pipelines.
method: Prompts LLMs to generate syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests for quantum programming tasks.
Injects candidate solutions at runtime and compares each test verdict against independent benchmark checker labels.
Uses three validation cohorts and oracle-verified synthetic mutants to evaluate test quality and bug-detection ability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors benchmarked five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks, with best test quality reaching 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval.
infographic.watch_item: High executability does not guarantee useful discrimination, so test suites should be validated against independent checkers rather than assumed correct.
infographic.paper_title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code

title: Transformer-based In-Context Score Operator Learning for Diffusion Models
authors: Wuzhe Xu, Zhaiming Shen, Yulong Lu, Wenjing Liao, Rongjie Lai
abstract: Diffusion models typically learn the generative dynamics of a single target distribution or a family of distributions indexed by conditioning variables fixed during training. This limits their ability to adapt to a previously unseen distribution from only a small set of examples. We introduce an in-context solution operator learning framework for diffusion models, in which each target distribution is treated as a task drawn from a meta-distribution and is specified at inference time by an empirical context set. Our method learns an in-context score operator that maps the context samples, a noisy query point, and the diffusion time to the task-dependent score, enabling reverse-diffusion sampling on unseen tasks without retraining or parameter updates. A key observation is that the task-dependent score admits a Gaussian-kernel conditional-mean representation. Its empirical Nadaraya--Watson approximation can be represented exactly by a model in our constructed transformer class, providing a principled foundation for the proposed query-dependent attention architecture. The operator is trained through amortized denoising score matching across task distributions. We establish generalization-error bounds that quantify the effects of the context size, the numbers of training tasks and within-task samples, model complexity, and intrinsic and ambient dimensions. Numerically, we evaluate the method on a range of scientific and visual datasets, including Navier-Stokes, ERA5 climate data, QuickDraw sketches, and Food-101. The results show that the proposed method performs well on relatively simple task families, while its performance degrades as task complexity increases, thereby illustrating both the promise and the limitations of in-context learning for diffusion models.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns diffusion models into in-context learners by conditioning the score function on a small set of task examples, allowing adaptation to unseen distributions without retraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables flexible generative modeling for scientific and vision tasks where each new scenario can be specified by a few samples instead of a full retraining pipeline.
method: Treat each target distribution as a task sampled from a meta-distribution and provide an empirical context set at inference.
Learn an in-context score operator that takes context samples, a noisy query point, and diffusion time to predict the task-dependent score.
Use a transformer-style query-dependent attention mechanism justified by a Gaussian-kernel conditional-mean / Nadaraya–Watson representation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method was evaluated on Navier-Stokes, ERA5 climate data, QuickDraw, and Food-101, showing strong results on simpler task families but weaker performance as task complexity increased.
infographic.watch_item: Performance can degrade on more complex task families, so context size, task diversity, and model capacity must be chosen carefully for reliable deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Transformer-based In-Context Score Operator Learning for Diffusion Models

title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
authors: Weiliang Chen, Song Liao
abstract: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.

infographic.key_insight: RATED improves AI tool retrieval by combining semantic matching with real-time reliability feedback, so agents can avoid failing tools during execution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method is practical for deployed AI agents because it adapts to API outages with minimal latency and without retraining the base retriever.
method: Frozen dual-encoder for semantic tool-query matching
Contrastive fine-tuning to improve retrieval quality
Lightweight contextual bandit re-ranker uses execution feedback to down-rank unreliable tools
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on EcoAgent with 5,172 real-world tools and 210,000+ query-tool pairs; results show a 52.2% relative MRR gain and fault selection rate dropping from 86.2% to 2.9% under 30% outage.
infographic.watch_item: The dynamic bandit re-ranking depends on timely execution feedback, so performance may degrade if reliability signals are sparse, delayed, or noisy.
infographic.paper_title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics

title: SafeDiSTL: Decomposing Joint Constraints for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Hongrui Zheng, Aditya Singh, Rahul Mangharam
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent tasks often impose constraints on a shared objective or collective safety. A team level violation cost function can measure this constraint outcome, but does not distinguish which agents' actions most strongly influence that violation. We present SafeDiSTL, a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that allows for credit assignment even with joint constraint measurements. We use Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to measure episode-level violation through running-maximum cost increments. Smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable dynamics provide action sensitivities, which allocate each cost increment across agents at the same decision time. These sensitivities account for delayed effects when weighting agents' shares of each cost increment. We study the framework in cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control tasks. SafeDiSTL achieves 1.6-5.1x the safe-success rate in transport, improves navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivers 50-68% more throughput in traffic when compared to constrained baselines. Results demonstrate a strong improvement of the learned policy in dealing with shared constraint while retaining the performance of unconstrained policies.

infographic.key_insight: SafeDiSTL turns a single team-level safety violation into per-agent credit assignments using STL robustness and action sensitivities, so constrained multi-agent RL can learn safer behavior without losing task performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is useful for safety-critical cooperative systems because it helps diagnose and steer which agents contribute most to joint constraint violations in transport, navigation, and traffic control.
method: Use Signal Temporal Logic robustness to measure episode-level constraint violation via running-maximum cost increments.
Compute smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable action sensitivities to distribute each cost increment across agents at the same decision time.
Account for delayed effects when weighting each agent’s share of joint safety cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control, SafeDiSTL improves safe-success rates by 1.6–5.1x, boosts navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and increases traffic throughput by 50–68% versus constrained baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on smooth differentiable dynamics and reliable STL-based robustness signals, so its effectiveness may be reduced in highly non-smooth or poorly modeled environments.
infographic.paper_title: SafeDiSTL: Decomposing Joint Constraints for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

title: A Baseline Assessment for the Agentic Web Technology Stack
authors: Vagner Figueredo de Santana, Diogo Cortiz
abstract: The fast pace in which protocols, frameworks, and technologies are being proposed for LLM-based agents results in a complex scenario for anyone aiming to create state-of-the-art AI solutions. Without an assessment on how different protocols, frameworks, and libraries work together to compose an Agentic Web solution, developers and organizations face different challenges (e.g., skilling, governance, infrastructure) even before becoming part of the Agentic Web ecosystem. In this context, we propose a system for performing Agentic Web evaluations called MASTIF (Multi-Agent System TestIng Framework) and present a baseline assessment of Agentic Web technologies, including 3 LLMs, 3 protocols, and 4 agent implementation frameworks, against 300 Mind2Web benchmark tasks. Results suggest that selecting a task-specific technology stack may result in gains of task completion rate, efficiency score, and social value stability scores; and reductions in verbosity and time to complete tasks. With the presented results, we expect to present a baseline in terms of metrics and results for this complex and fast evolving scenario for those aiming at designing, assessing, and developing multi-agent systems.

infographic.key_insight: A task-specific combination of LLMs, protocols, and agent frameworks can improve Agentic Web performance compared with a one-size-fits-all stack.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper provides a baseline evaluation framework and results that can guide architecture choices for building, governing, and scaling multi-agent web systems.
method: Built MASTIF (Multi-Agent System TestIng Framework) for evaluating Agentic Web systems.
Benchmarked 3 LLMs, 3 protocols, and 4 agent implementation frameworks.
Tested stack combinations on 300 Mind2Web tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved task completion, efficiency, and social value stability, along with reduced verbosity and time to complete tasks, across the evaluated technology stacks.
infographic.watch_item: The results are baseline-specific and may not generalize across other tasks, environments, or rapidly changing agent technologies.
infographic.paper_title: A Baseline Assessment for the Agentic Web Technology Stack
